vignette: Kwame sits on the edge of the leather chair, his posture rigid, shoulders hunched as if bracing for a strike. At eighteen, he wears a probationary police uniform that hangs slightly loose across his narrow frame. The fabric smells of starch and duty, a stark contrast to the faded jeans he used to wear before the academy. He traces the rim of his water glass with a thumb calloused from grip training, eyes fixed on the exit door. When the clinic's HVAC system clicks on, his breath catches. His head snaps toward the sound, muscles locking before he slowly exhales and looks back at his clinician. He does not mention the noise. He simply waits. The history he shares begins in a cramped living room when he was eight. It was not one loud incident but a slow accumulation of violence that shaped his nervous system. He remembers the heavy thud of fists against drywall, the shatter of glass, his mother's muffled pleas echoing down the hallway. By age nine, he had learned to move like smoke-sliding out of bed, pressing his back against the cold floorboards, holding his breath until the footsteps faded. He tells his clinician he stopped crying by age ten. "Crying just gave them a reason to keep going," he says, his voice flat. He began sleeping in the kitchen, near the door, always facing inward. The trauma did not announce itself with a single moment; it seeped into the foundation of his days. As he entered his teens, he gravitated toward structure. He joined a youth auxiliary program at sixteen, drawn to the promise of order and protection. By eighteen, he had passed the physical exams and enrolled as a probationary officer. The uniform gave him a sense of control he never possessed as a child. But the job pulls at the old wiring. During morning briefings, when voices rise in frustration, his pulse spikes. He catches himself scanning rooms for blind spots, checking corners, memorizing who clutches their bag a little too tightly. He tells his clinician he flinches when a veteran officer drops a clipboard during training. "I don't even know why," he admits, rubbing his forearm. "It's like my body remembers what my mind is trying to bury." Now, the weight of the badge sits uneasily alongside his quiet dread. At night, sleep fractures into short, tense bursts. If a car backfires on his way to patrol, he drops to a crouch behind a parked SUV, hand flying to his hip before he catches himself. He avoids bars, crowded markets, even the local community center where he used to play soccer. "Too many people, too much noise," he explains. When thoughts of his childhood home surface, a cold pressure builds behind his ribs. He stops himself from scrolling through old photos. "If I look, I might not stop," he says. During shifts, he stays rigidly formal with his superiors, overcompensating for the fear he still carries. He describes waking up drenched in sweat, heart hammering against his ribs like a trapped bird, the phantom sound of breaking glass still ringing in his ears. In this room, Kwame finally lowers his shoulders. He speaks in a measured but urgent register, tracing the weight of the duty he now holds. He talks about patrolling streets that feel too much like the ones he fled, the exhaustion of holding himself together while watching other people's crises unfold. He does not ask for advice. He simply needs someone to witness how heavy it is to stand guard while still waiting for the other shoe to drop. His clinician listens as the afternoon light shifts across the floor, noting how his hands rest openly on his knees now, how his breathing has slowed to match the rhythm of his own words. Kwame remains present, anchored in the quiet space between the uniform and the boy he once was.
